extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent applicants/practioners (patent attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing whether patent claims and amendments are supported by the original disclosure, and for identifying/prosecuting rejections or objections for lack of written description or introduction of new matter under 35 U.S.C. 112, 35 U.S.C. 132/251, and related provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support for amendments and added claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims or the addition of a new claim must be supported by the description of the invention in the application as filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An amendment to the specification (e.g., a change in the definition of a term used both in the specification and claim) may indirectly affect a claim even though no actual amendment is made to the claim. See In re Wright, 866 F.2d 422, 9 USPQ2d 1649 (Fed. Cir. 1989).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on filing date of parent application (35 U.S.C. 120)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims in a U.S. application are entitled to the benefit of the filing date of an earlier filed U.S. application only if the subject matter of the claim is disclosed in the manner provided by 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (or pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph) in the earlier application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites: Tronzo v. Biomet, Inc., 156 F.3d 1154; In re Scheiber, 587 F.2d 59. Examiner must determine whether the earlier application provides the written description support required for entitlement to parent filing date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on foreign or provisional priority (35 U.S.C. 119)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims are entitled to the benefit of a foreign priority date or provisional filing date only if the corresponding earlier application supports the claims in the manner required by 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (or pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites: In re Ziegler; Kawai v. Metlesics; In re Gosteli. The documentation and disclosure in the earlier-filed foreign or provisional application must provide the written description support for the claimed subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support for claims corresponding to an interference count
rubrics_metrics.description: In an interference, the claim corresponding to a count must be supported by the specification in the manner provided by 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (or pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A broad generic disclosure to a class of compounds is not sufficient written description for a specific compound within the class (Fields v. Conover). When seeking benefit of an earlier U.S. application in an interference, the earlier application must meet 35 U.S.C. 112(a) for the subject matter of the count (Hyatt v. Boone).

rubrics_metrics.name: Original claim may lack adequate written description
rubrics_metrics.description: An original claim may lack written description support when (1) it defines the invention in functional language specifying a desired result but the disclosure fails to sufficiently identify how the function is performed or the result is achieved, or (2) a broad genus claim is presented but the disclosure only describes a narrow species with no evidence that the genus is contemplated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Written description is not necessarily met even when claim language appears verbatim in the specification; mere indistinct words in a specification or claim do not satisfy the requirement. See Ariad Pharm. v. Eli Lilly; Enzo Biochem v. Gen‑Probe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indefiniteness of means‑/step‑plus‑function limitations (35 U.S.C. 112(f))
rubrics_metrics.description: A means‑(or step‑)plus‑function limitation shall be construed to cover the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification and equivalents. If the specification fails to disclose sufficient corresponding structure/materials/acts to perform the claimed function, the limitation is indefinite under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (pre‑AIA 112, second paragraph).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a limitation also may lack adequate written description under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) because an indefinite functional limitation could cover all ways of performing a function, indicating lack of possession. Authority: In re Donaldson Co.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden on the examiner re: written description requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The inquiry into whether the written description requirement is met is a question of fact; the description as filed is presumed adequate unless the examiner presents sufficient evidence or reasoning to rebut that presumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner has the initial burden of presenting, by a preponderance of evidence, why a person skilled in the art would not recognize in the disclosure a description of the invention defined by the claims. See In re Wertheim; In re Marzocchi.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statement of rejection requirements (what examiner must include)
rubrics_metrics.description: When rejecting a claim for lack of written description, the examiner must set forth express findings of fact supporting the conclusion (identify claim limitations at issue and establish a prima facie case with reasons).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Findings should: (A) Identify the claim limitation(s) at issue; and (B) Establish a prima facie case by providing reasons why one skilled in the art at the time of filing would not have recognized that the inventor was in possession of the claimed invention given the disclosure. A general allegation of unpredictability is insufficient. A concise statement identifying the unsupported limitation can sometimes be sufficient. See MPEP § 2163 and Hyatt v. Dudas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggesting claim/specification amendments (examiner practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: When appropriate, the examiner should suggest amendments to claims which can be supported by the application's written description, mindful of prohibition against adding new matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested amendments should avoid introducing new matter into claims or description. See Rasmussen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responding to applicant's reply (examiner duty before repeating rejection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon applicant's reply, the examiner must review the basis for any written description rejection in view of the whole record (including amendments, arguments, and evidence). If the record now demonstrates adequacy, do not repeat the rejection in the next Office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the record still fails to demonstrate adequacy, repeat the rejection fully, respond to rebuttal arguments, and properly treat any showings submitted in the reply. Affidavits relevant to the written description requirement must be thoroughly analyzed and discussed. See In re Alton.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changes to claim scope after filing require original support
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to meet written description commonly arises when claims are changed after filing to broaden or narrow breadth, alter a numerical range, or use terminology not synonymous with originally disclosed terminology; each claim limitation must be expressly, implicitly, or inherently supported in the originally filed disclosure to comply and to be entitled to earlier priority/filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 2163 for detailed examination guidelines. This applies also for entitlement under 35 U.S.C. 119, 120, or 365(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadening claims by omission of a limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Omitting a limitation can raise whether the inventor had possession of a broader, more generic invention; if the omitted element was described as essential or critical to the invention, omission will fail the written description requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/cases: Gentry Gallery v. Berkline (omission of location of control means); Tronzo v. Biomet (parent disclosed conical cup, later generic cup claim not entitled to parent date); In re Wilder. A claim that omits matter disclosed as essential may also be subject to rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (not enabling) or 112(b) (indefinite). See related cases and MPEP § 2172.01.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support for a genus via representative species (addition of generic claim)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed genus may be supported by sufficient description of a representative number of species; where the genus exhibits substantial variation, a sufficient variety of species must be described to reflect that variation. Disclosure of only one species supports a genus only if it indicates the patentee invented species sufficient to constitute the genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If evidence indicates ordinary artisans could not predict operability of species other than the one disclosed, genus is not supported (AbbVie v. Janssen; In re Curtis). In some situations a single species may suffice (In re Rasmussen; In re Herschler; In re Smythe). Case‑by‑case analysis; see cited authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrowing or subgeneric claim changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Introducing claim changes that narrow claims by adding elements or limitations not supported by the as‑filed disclosure violates the written description requirement; subgeneric terminology may or may not be acceptable depending on whether the disclosure reasonably communicates the subgenus to skilled artisans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Fujikawa v. Wattanasin (laundry list not sufficient), In re Ruschig, Rozbicki v. Chiang. Each situation decided on facts of what is reasonably communicated (In re Wilder).

rubrics_metrics.name: Changing numerical range limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: When changing numerical ranges, the analysis must consider which ranges one skilled in the art would consider inherently supported by the original disclosure; open‑ended changes may extend beyond the disclosed ranges and fail written description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: original spec disclosed 25%–60% and examples of 36% and 50%; a claim to ‘at least 35%’ (no upper bound) was not supported, whereas ‘between 35% and 60%’ was supported. See In re Wertheim; compare Union Oil v. Atl. Richfield and Purdue Pharma v. Faulding for additional contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationship of written description requirement to new matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Lack of written description generally arises with respect to claim subject matter; amendment of abstract, specification, or drawings raises new matter issues if the amendment content is not described in the application as filed. Information from any part of the original application may be added to any other part without introducing new matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two statutory provisions prohibit introduction of new matter: 35 U.S.C. 132 (no amendment shall introduce new matter) and 35 U.S.C. 251 (no new matter in reissue applications).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of new matter (examiner actions)
rubrics_metrics.description: If new subject matter is added to the disclosure, the examiner should object under 35 U.S.C. 132 or 251 as appropriate and require applicant to cancel the new matter; if new matter is added to claims, the examiner should reject the claims under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (written description).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When claims have not been amended but the specification is amended to add new matter, a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) should be made whenever claim limitations are affected by the added material. When an amendment is filed in reply to an objection/rejection, review the entire application to determine whether new matter is involved and require applicant to point out support for amendments. See In re Rasmussen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewability of new matter objections and rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejection of claims for new matter is reviewable by the Patent Trial and Appeal Board (PTAB); an objection and requirement to delete new matter is subject to supervisory review by petition under 37 CFR 1.181.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If both claims and specification contain new matter and there has been both a rejection and an objection, the issue is appealable and should not be decided by petition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claimed subject matter disclosed only in claims (antecedent/support issues)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims as filed are part of the disclosure; if the original specification lacks the remainder support for originally filed claim material, the applicant may amend the specification to include the claimed subject matter (use form paragraph 7.44 where originally claimed subject matter lacks proper antecedent basis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See In re Benno. Examiner should consider that claims form part of the original disclosure and allow specification amendment to provide necessary support where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendments supported in the original description are not new matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Amendments to an application which are supported in the original description do NOT constitute new matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the amendment does not add information beyond what the original disclosure conveyed (expressly, implicitly, or inherently), it is permissible. See MPEP § 2163.07.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rephrasing and dictionary/definition inclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere rephrasing of a passage that preserves the same meaning does not constitute new matter; inclusion of dictionary or art‑recognized definitions known at filing may not be new matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If multiple definitions for a term exist and a definition is added later, it must be clear from the application as filed that the applicant intended that particular definition to avoid new matter or lack of written description (Scarring Corp. v. Megan, Inc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Correction of obvious errors
rubrics_metrics.description: An amendment to correct an obvious error does not constitute new matter where one skilled in the art would recognize the error and the appropriate correction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See In re Odd. Exception: where a foreign priority document is of record, applicant may not rely on that foreign disclosure to support correction of an error in the pending U.S. application unless the U.S. application explicitly incorporates the foreign document by reference. See Ex parte Bondiou and related guidance on incorporation by reference (37 CFR 1.55; 1.57(a); MPEP § 217).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherent functions, theories, or advantages
rubrics_metrics.description: By disclosing a device that inherently performs a function, has a property, operates according to a theory, or has an advantage, a patent application necessarily discloses that inherent function/theory/advantage even if not stated explicitly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The application may later be amended to recite the inherent function/theory/advantage without introducing prohibited new matter. Authorities: In re Reynolds; In re Smythe.
